newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Long term benefit from China-Taiwan flights - Cathay.
newsitem.headline: Long term benefit from China-Taiwan flights - Cathay.

text.p: Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd may suffer a short-term negative impact should direct flights between Taiwan and mainland China be opened, but would benefit long term, chairman Peter Sutch said on Wednesday.

"It would be naive to say that we would not feel some impact at least in the short term, but in the longer term...we would expect there to be a much bigger cake," Sutch told a news conference following release the group's 1996 results.
"Although we (may get) a smaller slice of that cake in the sense of not all traffic having to flow this way to Hong Kong, in the long run we would welcome that development," he said.

Direct flights are currently banned between political rivals Taiwan and China, forcing much of the passenger and freight between the two to flow through Hong Kong, but the ban is expected to be lifted sometime in the not too distant future.

Sutch said such a development -- direct flights between the two areas -- would herald an improvement in economic and other spheres and "an all together more stable environment in this part of the world."
"It is a very complex and sensitive issue and if a resolution is found to it, it will mean a major step forward.

"We believe that it will mean we are going to see a substantial growth over a period of time in the volume of passenger and cargo. We believe that it is not all going to happen overnight. It would obviously be a major build up and that it is manageable," he added.
Sutch also noted deals that brought greater Chinese participation in Cathay and Hong Kong's aviation industry had been positive for the group.

CITIC Pacific Ltd last June subscribed for 572.9 million new Cathay shares and boosted its holding in the airline to 25 percent from 10 percent, cutting the holding of parent Swire Pacific Ltd to 43.86 percent from 52.63 percent. "(This) raised some HK$6.2 billion which has effectively all been reinvested or is committed to be reinvested in the business, largely in the new airport," said Sutch, referring to the proceeds from the new share issue.
China National Aviation Corp of China also took a 35.88 percent stake in Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Ltd, buying shares from CITIC Pacific and from Swire and Cathay.
These were major and very welcome developments for Cathay, said Sutch.
"All of this has helped to create a more certain, stable aviation environment here in which we can continue to make major investment decisions," said Sutch.
Prior to the deals there were concerns that British-owned Cathay could suffer following Hong Kong's handover to China at midnight of June 30 this year.
Sutch has previously said he saw business as usual or even better than usual after the transition.
